extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, law clerks, and in-house counsel working on SEP/FRAND litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of legal standards and evidentiary criteria from a Federal Circuit opinion addressing jury unanimity, patent-eligibility (§101), means-plus-function (§112 ¶6), claim construction, FRAND/SEP damages, and admissibility of settlement evidence. Useful for practitioners preparing or evaluating appellate and trial strategy in SEP litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury unanimity requirement for each legal claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The Seventh Amendment preserves the right to a jury trial and unanimity is required where the Seventh Amendment applies; Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 48(b) states that, unless the parties stipulate otherwise, the verdict must be unanimous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unanimity must obtain on the ultimate legal result of each claim, not just on a general verdict. A verdict form that permits the jury to find liability by aggregating different jurors’ beliefs that different patents (or different causes of action) were infringed (e.g., asking whether defendant infringed "ANY" of the asserted claims) violates the unanimity requirement. The verdict form must, at minimum, include separate infringement questions for each asserted patent unless the issue of infringement is truly identical across the patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each asserted patent is a distinct cause of action
rubrics_metrics.description: In the patent context, each patent asserted raises an independent and distinct cause of action, and therefore infringement must be separately proved as to each patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple patents are asserted, the court should not 'interweave' causes of action on a single question that covers multiple patents. Verdict forms and instructions should permit the jury to render unanimous findings on each asserted patent (or otherwise ensure unanimity per cause of action). Cited authority: Kearns v. Gen. Motors Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse-of-discretion review for verdict form design
rubrics_metrics.description: The verdict form is reviewed for an abuse of discretion; district courts have broad authority and discretion in controlling the conduct of a trial, including the form by which juries return verdicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A district court abuses its discretion when its exercise of discretion is guided by an erroneous legal conclusion. Courts should ensure verdict forms allow the jury to announce the ultimate legal result of each claim. (Cites: R.R. Dynamics; Koon.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Verdict form must announce ultimate legal result of each claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'key' to a general verdict is whether the jury announces the ultimate legal result of each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the verdict form asks an overly broad question (e.g., whether defendant infringed 'any' asserted claims) it may fail this test. The form should break out infringement at least patent-by-patent (or more narrowly claim-by-claim if appropriate) so the jury's unanimous determination on each cause of action is clear. (Discusses Zhang v. Am. Gem Seafoods and Jazzabi v. Allstate.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages cannot be awarded absent an infringement finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages must be based on a finding of infringement; unless and until plaintiff proves infringement at a new trial, there is no infringement finding on which damages can be awarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the infringement finding is vacated, any damages award that assumes infringement must also be vacated. A damages retrial that instructs the jury to assume infringement of patents when the infringement verdict is defective is erroneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of FRAND-encumbered SEPs in damages trials
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserted patents are FRAND-encumbered SEPs, any royalty awarded must be FRAND; the jury must be informed of the FRAND commitments and must hear evidence about what royalties would or could be FRAND.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding evidence of the patent-holder's FRAND obligations or failing to instruct the jury on FRAND commitments undermines the reliability of a damages verdict and can warrant a new trial. (Cites Ericsson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of settlement agreements as comparable licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior settlement agreements may be used to establish reasonable royalties under certain limited circumstances, but their propriety is questionable and they must be economically comparable and probative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts must exercise vigilance when considering past licenses or settlement agreements to technologies other than the patent in suit. A settlement agreement that has little relation to the economic demand for the patented technology or whose scope is far greater than the hypothetical license is likely inadmissible. (Cites LaserDynamics; ResQNet.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Rule of Evidence 403 balancing for prejudicial evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The court may exclude relevant evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay, wasting time, or needlessly presenting cumulative evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a settlement agreement (or expert testimony about it) is presented that contains very large dollar figures or is not sufficiently comparable, the risk of unfair prejudice (e.g., skewing the jury’s damages horizon) can substantially outweigh any probative value and warrant exclusion under Rule 403. Precedents applying this balancing include LaserDynamics and Uniloc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors making a settlement agreement non-comparable
rubrics_metrics.description: A settlement/license may be non-comparable (and thus of minimal probative value) when its scope of patent rights is far greater than the asserted patents, when it resolves global litigation across multiple claim types (patent, antitrust, trade-secret, tort), or when it does not actually license the asserted patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert testimony relying on such a settlement as a 'check' or 'ballpark' must meaningfully account for differences in scope; failure to do so weakens probative value and increases unfair prejudice. Emphasis of large settlement figures to the jury can be especially prejudicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony admitting non-comparable agreements must be reliable and apportionable
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert relying on settlement agreements must acknowledge and adjust for differences in comparability and use reliable methodology to apportion value attributable to the patented features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the expert admits the settlement is not economically comparable, or fails to account for non-patent components and scope differences, the testimony is unreliable and may be excluded as unfairly prejudicial or misleading. (Cites Ericsson; Uniloc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Review standards for patent eligibility and claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and claim construction are legal questions reviewed de novo (though eligibility may involve underlying factual issues). For non-patent procedural matters, apply regional circuit law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent eligibility is reviewed de novo, but courts may consider factual issues underlying the §101 analysis. The opinion applied Fifth Circuit law for non-patent issues (evidentiary/abuse-of-discretion), and Fed. Cir. law for claim construction and §112 ¶6 legal framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 101 'directed to an abstract idea' inquiry (eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be held patent-ineligible under § 101 if it is directed to an abstract idea; the court applies the governing § 101 framework (including assessing whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts' grant/denial of summary judgment on § 101 is reviewed de novo; identification of abstract idea requires careful analysis of claim language and may be dispositive of invalidity. (The opinion reversed the district court's non-abstract finding for claims 6 and 7 of the ’332 patent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (§ 112 ¶6) two-step analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Determine whether the claim term is in means-plus-function format; absence of the word 'means' creates a rebuttable presumption that § 112 ¶6 does not apply. Step 2: If § 112 ¶6 applies, determine whether the specification discloses adequate corresponding structure for the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption may be overcome if the challenger shows the claim term fails to recite sufficiently definite structure or recites function without sufficient structure. Generic nonce terms (e.g., 'unit', 'module', 'mechanism', 'device') often do not connote structure and may invoke § 112 ¶6. If § 112 ¶6 applies, remand to the district court is appropriate to determine corresponding structure in the first instance. (Cites Williamson, Diebold Nixdorf, MPEP §2181.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic 'unit' terminology may invoke § 112 ¶6
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'unit,' 'module,' 'mechanism,' and 'device' are generic placeholders that often do not connote sufficiently definite structure and thus can be treated like 'means' under § 112 ¶6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the term is modified (e.g., 'selecting unit'), if the modifier and surrounding language are purely functional (e.g., 'configured to randomly select') and no structure is described, the presumption against § 112 ¶6 can be overcome. Prior district-court holdings finding structure are not controlling if contradicted by intrinsic record or parties' own positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain meaning, lexicography, and disclaimer in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim language has its ordinary meaning unless the patentee acts as lexicographer or disavows claim scope in the specification or prosecution history; absent lexicography or disavowal, courts should not depart from plain meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To import limits into a claim or depart from plain meaning, there must be clear expressions of intent in the specification or prosecution history. (Cites GE Lighting Sols.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand where district court must make factual findings on corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When an appellate court determines a claim term invokes § 112 ¶6, the matter of whether the specification discloses adequate corresponding structure is a factual/intrinsic-record determination for the district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts should remand such issues for the district court to conduct the § 112 ¶6 step-two analysis in the first instance rather than resolve corresponding-structure questions on appeal.
